To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the strain-induced changes in the hydrogen adsorptive properties of the low-index Cu surface can be explained by the strain-induced changes of the local density of states at the adsorption sites, and that the strain-induced change of the hydrogen adsorption and dissociative properties of the oxygen-covered Cu(1 0 0) surface can be related to the hydrogen–oxygen separation distance.

the adsorption of hydrogen and oxygen on Cu surfaces is affected by lattice strain in different ways and that the dissociation barrier for hydrogen on Cu(100) can be reduced significantly by preadsorption of oxygen.

the dissociation of hydrogen is enhanced by lattice expansion of Cu surfaces and that the strain-induced change of the hydrogen adsorption energy and dissociation barrier can be rationalized by taking into account the adsorbate–substrate interaction and the change of the local d-band center.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel materials for the production of hydrogen from water.
the adsorption and dissociative chemisorption of H _{2} molecules on clean and O-covered Cu surfaces.
the electronic structure and the reactivity of strained Cu surfaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the strain-induced change of the adsorption energy and dissociation barrier for the hydrogen adsorption on the clean Cu(1 10) surface cannot be rationalized in terms of a simple d-band picture.

the strain-induced change of the hydrogen adsorption and dissociative adsorption on the low-index Cu surface is not a straightforward effect of the strain-induced change on the d-band center of the surface Cu atoms.
the d-band model does not provide a general and simple description for the adsorption and dissociative adsorption of atomic hydrogen on strained Cu(1 0 0) and Cu(1 1 1) surfaces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the d-band center is not the most important factor to determine the adsorbate binding strength.
the d-band model does not work for hydrogen adsorption/dissorption on strained Cu surfaces, but it does work for oxygen-precovered Cu(1 0 0) surfaces.
strain-induced changes in the adsorption and reaction properties of hydrogen on Cu surfaces are not as simple as the d-band model suggests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the d-band model cannot be used to rationalize trends in the adsorption energies and the dissociation barriers of hydrogen on strained surfaces.
the d-band model does not work well for the dissociative adsorption of H2 on strained Cu surfaces.
the d-band model does not always work for the dissociative adsorption of H2 on metal surfaces.
